contrastMetadata.transferBoundary: For one sequential objective, avoid preprocessing that is not reused; for many static interval queries, compare full prefix build-plus-query cost, while updates may invalidate the static prefix representation.

items.prompt: An unsorted static array receives exactly one query for the sum of a known interval [l, r], and no later reuse is possible. Which baseline is usually sufficient?

options.text: Scan the requested interval once.
Always build an O(n)-space prefix array first.
Enumerate every possible window before answering.
Sort the interval before summing.

feedback.reason: One unrepeated query does not automatically justify a reusable index.

blocks.text: Compare the complete workload

Let m = r - l + 1. Starting a running sum at zero and visiting a[l], ..., a[r] reads exactly m values, so the query costs O(m) time and O(1) auxiliary space. Building P[i + 1] = P[i] + a[i] would first read all n values and retain n + 1 cumulative sums; it would then answer this one query as P[r + 1] - P[l]. Because the prompt rules out later reuse, that O(n)-time, O(n)-space index provides no subsequent benefit. The scan is therefore the sufficient baseline, especially when m is much smaller than n.

blocks.title: Preprocessing must earn its cost
blocks.text: Do not choose a prefix array merely because there are several intervals. Count build time, the cost of all queries, the length of direct scans, memory, and whether the source changes. Prefix state is valuable when compatible static queries reuse it; a one-pass local workload usually gains more from direct or rolling state.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.prefix_mandatory: A prefix array is legal, but it spends O(n) build time and O(n) space to save work on only one interval; the prompt provides no later query that could amortize that state.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sliding_all: Enumerating all n - m + 1 length-m windows solves a different workload. Only the already known interval [l, r] must be summed.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_range: Addition does not depend on element order, so sorting cannot make the sum easier and costs extra time; an in-place sort would also destroy the array's original index order.

items.prompt: An immutable n-value array will receive q arbitrary range-sum queries. Which workload expression supports prefix sums?

options.text: O(n) preprocessing followed by O(1) arithmetic per query.
One moving window is O(1) regardless of how far query boundaries jump.
Sorting once makes original interval sums constant-time.
Every query is free because the array is static.

feedback.reason: Prefix state separates one build cost from repeated query cost.

blocks.text: Compare the complete workload

Build a length-(n + 1) array with P[0] = 0 and P[i + 1] = P[i] + a[i]. This preprocessing visits each source value once, so it costs O(n) time and O(n) auxiliary space. An inclusive query [l, r] is then P[r + 1] - P[l]: the shared contribution before l cancels, leaving exactly the requested interval in O(1) time. Across q arbitrary queries on the same immutable version, total time is O(n) + q·O(1) = O(n + q), while the prefix array remains O(n) live state.

blocks.title: Preprocessing must earn its cost
blocks.text: Do not choose a prefix array merely because there are several intervals. Count build time, the cost of all queries, the length of direct scans, memory, and whether the source changes. Prefix state is valuable when compatible static queries reuse it; a one-pass local workload usually gains more from direct or rolling state.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.move_between_queries: A moving sum is constant-time only for a bounded boundary change such as shifting one position. Arbitrary consecutive ranges can move their endpoints across Θ(n) values.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_once: Sorting changes which values occupy the original indices, so a sum over sorted positions no longer answers the requested original interval.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.scan_free: Immutability makes cached state reusable; it does not create that state. Without an index, the values in each requested interval still have to be visited.

items.prompt: The task asks for the maximum sum over every length-k block, visited from left to right exactly once. Which repeated-workload choice is strongest?

options.text: Use one rolling sum in O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary state.
A prefix array is the only valid way to reuse work.
Rescan k elements for every block.
Treat each block as an unrelated random query.

feedback.reason: Many intervals do not automatically imply prefix preprocessing.

blocks.text: Compare the complete workload

First sum a[0..k - 1] and use it to initialize the maximum. When the block shifts from [i, i + k - 1] to [i + 1, i + k], subtract the unique outgoing value a[i] and add the unique incoming value a[i + k], then compare the new sum with the maximum. The initialization costs O(k), and the n - k shifts cost O(1) each, for O(n) total time. On an indexable array, the current sum, maximum, and indices are O(1) auxiliary state. A prefix array could also answer every block in O(n) total time, but its O(n) retained state is not required for this one ordered traversal.

blocks.title: Preprocessing must earn its cost
blocks.text: Do not choose a prefix array merely because there are several intervals. Count build time, the cost of all queries, the length of direct scans, memory, and whether the source changes. Prefix state is valuable when compatible static queries reuse it; a one-pass local workload usually gains more from direct or rolling state.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.prefix_only: Prefix sums are valid, but they are not the only reusable state: adjacent equal-length blocks differ by exactly one outgoing and one incoming value.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.scan_each: Rescanning all k positions for each of n - k + 1 blocks repeats their overlap and costs Θ((n - k + 1)k) rather than one linear traversal.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.query_count: The blocks are not unrelated random queries. Their endpoints advance together by one, which is precisely the transition a rolling sum can reuse.

items.prompt: After each point update, later range sums must reflect the new value. What is the main issue with a plain static prefix array?

options.text: Changing a[i] invalidates every stored prefix after i, so rebuilding or another dynamic structure is required.
Prefix subtraction cannot handle positive values after an update.
Every dynamic range query becomes a sliding-window problem.
Sorting repairs all prefixes.

feedback.reason: Static prefix state encodes cumulative values of one array version.

blocks.text: Compare the complete workload

For P[j] = a[0] + ... + a[j - 1], a change at a[i] contributes to every P[j] with j > i. If a[i] changes by delta, that entire stored suffix must also change by delta; leaving it untouched makes later subtraction return sums from the old array version. Updating a plain prefix array can therefore take Θ(n - i), and rebuilding it takes Θ(n). When both point updates and arbitrary range sums are frequent, a dynamic cumulative structure such as a Fenwick tree or segment tree can support each operation in O(log n) instead of pretending the static prefixes remain valid.

blocks.title: Preprocessing must earn its cost
blocks.text: Do not choose a prefix array merely because there are several intervals. Count build time, the cost of all queries, the length of direct scans, memory, and whether the source changes. Prefix state is valuable when compatible static queries reuse it; a one-pass local workload usually gains more from direct or rolling state.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.query_wrong_sign: The identity P[r + 1] - P[l] works for positive, zero, and negative values. The failure is stale cumulative state, not a sign restriction.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.window_required: Mutation does not turn arbitrary interval requests into one locally advancing interval. A dynamic range-query structure may be the appropriate representation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_update: Sorting neither applies the update delta to stored prefixes nor preserves the original interval indices, so it cannot repair the representation.

items.prompt: A query workload asks for the sum of the most recent k stream values after every arrival. Why is a prefix array not automatically the best fit?

options.text: Only one frontier-local interval is needed, so a rolling sum can answer online with bounded state.
Prefix sums cannot represent stream prefixes.
The stream is immutable before it arrives.
A rolling window answers arbitrary historical ranges for free.

feedback.reason: Query count alone is not the decision boundary.

blocks.text: Compare the complete workload

After arrival t, the requested interval is always the frontier [t - k + 1, t]. Maintain its sum by adding the new value and, once more than k values have arrived, subtracting the value that just left. In a true one-pass stream that outgoing value cannot be reread from the source, so a queue or ring buffer retains at most k values: O(1) update time, O(k) retained values, and one scalar sum. Appended prefix sums could answer the same interval as P[t + 1] - P[t - k + 1], but retaining every prefix grows with the stream length. They are useful only if later historical ranges also need answers.

blocks.title: Preprocessing must earn its cost
blocks.text: Do not choose a prefix array merely because there are several intervals. Count build time, the cost of all queries, the length of direct scans, memory, and whether the source changes. Prefix state is valuable when compatible static queries reuse it; a one-pass local workload usually gains more from direct or rolling state.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.prefix_incorrect: Prefix sums can represent an append-only stream. The objection is that keeping the full history is unnecessary for a frontier-only last-k workload.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.queries_static: Already arrived values may be stable, but future values do not exist yet; that fact does not turn the online workload into static preprocessing.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.window_random: A rolling state represents only its current interval. It cannot recover an arbitrary old [l, r] after those values have been discarded.

items.prompt: Only two short interval queries will be asked on a very large array. Which conclusion is defensible?

options.text: Compare the total scanned lengths with O(n) prefix construction instead of assuming preprocessing wins.
Any q greater than one requires prefix sums.
A sliding window is always optimal for two queries.
Query volume never affects strategy.

feedback.reason: The relevant direct cost is the sum of queried interval lengths.

blocks.text: Compare the complete workload

If the two interval lengths are m1 and m2, direct scans visit m1 + m2 values and use O(1) auxiliary space. Prefix preprocessing visits all n values, retains O(n) cumulative state, and then spends O(1) per query, for O(n + 2) time. Thus the relevant comparison is m1 + m2 versus n + 2, together with the memory budget. When both intervals are short relative to a very large n and no other consumer needs prefixes, direct scans can be decisively cheaper even though q = 2.

blocks.title: Preprocessing must earn its cost
blocks.text: Do not choose a prefix array merely because there are several intervals. Count build time, the cost of all queries, the length of direct scans, memory, and whether the source changes. Prefix state is valuable when compatible static queries reuse it; a one-pass local workload usually gains more from direct or rolling state.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.prefix_always: The inequality q > 1 says nothing about interval lengths. Two tiny scans may cost far less than reading and storing all n values.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.window_always: A rolling window helps only when consecutive ranges have a cheap predictable transition; two arbitrary intervals may be far apart or have different lengths.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.ignore_q: Query volume affects how often preprocessing can be reused. It matters, but it must be evaluated with lengths, updates, and memory rather than used alone.

items.prompt: A valid prefix array is persisted with the same immutable data version. A batch of new queries arrives. What should the cost model do?

options.text: Treat preprocessing as already paid and count only the new query work.
Charge another O(n) build for every batch by definition.
Use the prefix array even if the data version changed.
Discard the prefix array because windows are always linear.

feedback.reason: Workload analysis starts from the actual available state.

blocks.text: Compare the complete workload

The persisted prefix array already encodes this exact immutable version, so the incremental cost of the new batch is q constant-time differences, O(q), with no new build. The original O(n) preprocessing still belongs in a report of the representation's total lifetime cost, but it is a sunk cost for the current routing decision. Rebuilding an identical valid index would duplicate work. Before reusing it, verify a version identifier or equivalent invariant; if the source changed, P[r + 1] - P[l] would combine stale cumulative values and the saved build cannot be credited.

blocks.title: Preprocessing must earn its cost
blocks.text: Do not choose a prefix array merely because there are several intervals. Count build time, the cost of all queries, the length of direct scans, memory, and whether the source changes. Prefix state is valuable when compatible static queries reuse it; a one-pass local workload usually gains more from direct or rolling state.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.rebuild_each_batch: Batch boundaries do not invalidate state. Rebuilding the same verified representation adds O(n) work without changing any answer.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.ignore_version: The prefix entries are functions of one exact source version; a mismatch makes their differences stale even if query syntax is unchanged.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.switch_window: A linear rolling traversal is not automatically cheaper than q O(1) lookups from an already available index, especially for arbitrary ranges.

items.prompt: Future query count is unknown and may remain zero. Which strategy can avoid unnecessary preprocessing?

options.text: Answer early queries directly, then build prefix state only if a stable version reaches a defined demand threshold.
Build every possible index immediately regardless of demand.
Unknown q makes a strategy impossible.
Sort after every query.

feedback.reason: A lazy policy can defer the O(n) build until there is evidence of reuse.

blocks.text: Compare the complete workload

Start with no index, so a workload that receives zero queries pays zero preprocessing cost. For each direct query, track its scanned length and keep prefix state absent while cumulative demand is small. A deterministic policy can trigger a build after observed work reaches a chosen threshold comparable to the O(n) build, provided the same data version is still expected to serve queries. Past scans are sunk and do not guarantee future demand, so the threshold is an adaptive risk policy, not proof that the next query will repay construction. Build at most once per version, validate that version, and route only later compatible queries through it.

blocks.title: Preprocessing must earn its cost
blocks.text: Do not choose a prefix array merely because there are several intervals. Count build time, the cost of all queries, the length of direct scans, memory, and whether the source changes. Prefix state is valuable when compatible static queries reuse it; a one-pass local workload usually gains more from direct or rolling state.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.eager_always: If no compatible query arrives, every eagerly built index is pure unused time and memory.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.no_analysis: Unknown future demand prevents a perfect offline choice, but it still permits an explicit adaptive threshold with measurable worst-case cost.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_later: Sorting changes original index membership and does not create cumulative sums for the requested ranges.

items.prompt: Which workload facts belong in the one-query-versus-many decision? Select all that apply.

options.text: Number of queries.
Total or expected lengths of directly scanned intervals.
Update frequency and representation invalidation.
Only whether the prompt says contiguous.

feedback.reason: The decision is a lifecycle cost model.

blocks.text: Compare the complete workload

Let q be the number of queries and L the sum of their interval lengths. Direct scans cost O(L); a static prefix representation costs O(n + q) time and O(n) retained space, before counting any rebuilds caused by updates or version replacement. Therefore q matters because it controls possible reuse, interval lengths matter because they determine the actual direct work, and mutations matter because they can invalidate cumulative state. The word “contiguous” is only a shape property shared by both strategies. It does not reveal whether boundaries are arbitrary, whether preprocessing will be reused, or whether the source stays compatible.

blocks.title: Preprocessing must earn its cost
blocks.text: Do not choose a prefix array merely because there are several intervals. Count build time, the cost of all queries, the length of direct scans, memory, and whether the source changes. Prefix state is valuable when compatible static queries reuse it; a one-pass local workload usually gains more from direct or rolling state.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.contiguous_word: Both a direct or rolling scan and prefix subtraction can operate on contiguous intervals. That word omits the workload and lifetime facts that decide between them.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.query_count: More compatible queries create more opportunities to amortize one O(n) build; very few may leave it unrecovered.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.query_lengths: Direct cost is the sum of visited lengths L, which may be far smaller than the coarse worst-case bound qn.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.data_updates: A point update changes a suffix of plain prefixes, and a version replacement invalidates all of them, so rebuild work can dominate.

items.prompt: Which workloads strongly favor static prefix preprocessing? Select all that apply.

options.text: Many arbitrary range-sum queries over unchanged data.
Repeated query batches reuse the same verified data version.
Several additive interval metrics are queried repeatedly.
Only the most recent k stream values are queried online.

feedback.reason: Prefix preprocessing is strongest when static cumulative state is reused broadly.

blocks.text: Compare the complete workload

Prefix preprocessing retains a cumulative boundary for every source position, so its cost is best recovered by repeated requests that may choose arbitrary boundaries. Many random queries on unchanged data reuse that index directly. Repeated batches extend the same reuse across time, provided a version check proves the stored prefixes still match. Several repeatedly queried additive metrics can each have a compatible prefix array, trading additional O(n) state per metric for O(1) interval arithmetic. By contrast, a last-k stream workload requests only the current frontier interval; a rolling sum plus the outgoing-value buffer retains only the history needed for that moving boundary.

blocks.title: Preprocessing must earn its cost
blocks.text: Do not choose a prefix array merely because there are several intervals. Count build time, the cost of all queries, the length of direct scans, memory, and whether the source changes. Prefix state is valuable when compatible static queries reuse it; a one-pass local workload usually gains more from direct or rolling state.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.single_last_k: This workload never asks for arbitrary historical boundaries. Retaining every prefix grows with stream history, whereas a rolling sum and at most k buffered values serve the frontier directly.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.many_random: After one O(n) build, each arbitrary [l, r] sum becomes the O(1) difference P[r + 1] - P[l].
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.repeated_batches: A verified unchanged version allows the same build cost to be amortized over every later compatible batch.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.multiple_metrics: Each additive metric can store its own cumulative array; repeated interval queries can justify the corresponding time-space tradeoff.

items.prompt: Which workloads favor a moving or direct approach over a prefix array? Select all that apply.

options.text: One short interval query with no later reuse.
All fixed-size windows are visited sequentially once.
A last-k stream answer is required after each arrival.
Millions of random range queries over immutable data.

feedback.reason: Moving or direct state is strongest when preprocessing is not reused or candidates evolve locally.

blocks.text: Compare the complete workload

For one interval of length m, a direct scan spends O(m) without an O(n) index that will never be reused. For every adjacent length-k block on an indexable array, a rolling aggregate uses the one-out/one-in transition and O(1) auxiliary state. For a true last-k stream, the same transition produces each answer online while retaining only the running sum and at most k values needed to identify future departures. These cases favor local state for different reasons: no reuse, predictable sequential reuse, or bounded online history. Millions of arbitrary ranges over immutable data have none of those restrictions and repeatedly benefit from prefix subtraction.

blocks.title: Preprocessing must earn its cost
blocks.text: Do not choose a prefix array merely because there are several intervals. Count build time, the cost of all queries, the length of direct scans, memory, and whether the source changes. Prefix state is valuable when compatible static queries reuse it; a one-pass local workload usually gains more from direct or rolling state.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.many_random_static: Arbitrary boundaries do not form one cheap moving transition, while immutability keeps a prefix index valid across all queries; this is a strong preprocessing case.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.one_short_query: Scanning its m values can cost far less than building and retaining cumulative state for all n positions.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.all_adjacent_fixed: Each next block removes one known value and adds one known value, so overlap yields an O(1) transition.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.online_frontier: A bounded moving state can emit the latest answer immediately; a complete historical index is unnecessary unless old ranges will also be queried.

items.prompt: Which changes can invalidate or weaken prefix reuse? Select all that apply.

options.text: Point updates to the source array.
Loading a different data version.
Queries switch from sum to a non-additive property not represented by the prefixes.
The same range-sum workload receives more queries.

feedback.reason: A precomputed representation is useful only while its source and represented operation remain valid.

blocks.text: Compare the complete workload

A prefix array is a materialized claim about both data and operation: P[j] stores the additive aggregate of one exact source version up to boundary j. A point update at i changes every later prefix; replacing the source changes the entire claim. Switching to a property that cannot be recovered by subtracting the stored additive prefixes makes the representation operationally incompatible even when the values themselves are unchanged. In contrast, an additional range-sum query on the same version changes neither data nor operation. It simply reuses the already valid state and increases the value obtained from its build.

blocks.title: Preprocessing must earn its cost
blocks.text: Do not choose a prefix array merely because there are several intervals. Count build time, the cost of all queries, the length of direct scans, memory, and whether the source changes. Prefix state is valuable when compatible static queries reuse it; a one-pass local workload usually gains more from direct or rolling state.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.more_queries: More queries with the same additive operation and source version do not invalidate anything; they strengthen amortization of the existing build.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.point_updates: Changing a[i] changes every cumulative P[j] with j > i, so leaving the suffix untouched returns stale sums.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.version_change: The stored cumulative values describe the previous version and cannot be safely paired with the replacement.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.new_metric: Subtraction recovers only operations represented by the stored cumulative state; a new non-additive property may need a different structure.

items.prompt: Arrange the workload comparison for direct scans versus prefix sums.

elements.text: Define n, query count q, interval lengths, updates, and required outputs.
Sum the direct work across all queried intervals.
Add prefix construction, compatible query work, and rebuilds.
Choose the legal path under time, space, and version-lifetime constraints.

feedback.reason: The comparison must count complete work on both paths.

blocks.text: Compare the complete workload

items: Define the actual lifecycle: source length n, query count q, every interval length mi, update or version-change frequency, output timing, and the memory limit.
Derive direct work as the total number of visited elements, L = m1 + ... + mq, plus only the constant state needed for one running sum.
Derive prefix work as O(n) construction plus O(q) compatible queries, O(n) retained state, and O(n) rebuilding for each version whose cumulative values must be replaced.
Eliminate timing- or version-illegal choices, then compare L with the full prefix lifecycle cost under the available time and space budgets.

blocks.text: Starting from q alone wrongly treats two tiny ranges like two full-array scans. Comparing before accounting for updates treats stale prefixes as reusable, while choosing before checking output timing can select an offline build for a query that must be answered before preprocessing is possible.

blocks.title: Preprocessing must earn its cost
blocks.text: Do not choose a prefix array merely because there are several intervals. Count build time, the cost of all queries, the length of direct scans, memory, and whether the source changes. Prefix state is valuable when compatible static queries reuse it; a one-pass local workload usually gains more from direct or rolling state.

items.prompt: Arrange a static prefix-query lifecycle.

elements.text: Confirm the source data version is immutable for the representation's lifetime.
Answer each compatible interval query by subtraction.
Discard or rebuild when the source version changes.

feedback.reason: Prefix state is tied to one exact source version.

blocks.text: Compare the complete workload

items: Bind the representation to an exact source version and confirm that this version will remain immutable while its queries are served.
Build P[0] = 0 and P[i + 1] = P[i] + a[i] once for that verified version.
For every compatible inclusive range [l, r], return P[r + 1] - P[l], which cancels the contribution before l.
When mutation or replacement changes the version, stop serving queries from P and either discard it or rebuild from the new source before reuse.

blocks.text: Building before identifying the version can publish state with no stable owner. Answering before construction reads missing cumulative boundaries, and continuing after a change silently returns sums from the old array. Discarding a still-valid index too early instead wastes the reuse that justified preprocessing.

blocks.title: Preprocessing must earn its cost
blocks.text: Do not choose a prefix array merely because there are several intervals. Count build time, the cost of all queries, the length of direct scans, memory, and whether the source changes. Prefix state is valuable when compatible static queries reuse it; a one-pass local workload usually gains more from direct or rolling state.

items.prompt: Arrange a lazy-preprocessing policy.

elements.text: Serve initial queries directly while tracking cumulative scan work.
Compare accumulated direct cost with prefix build and future expected demand.
Construct prefix state when the threshold is met and data is stable.
Route later compatible queries through the verified prefix representation.

feedback.reason: Lazy construction avoids paying for unused preprocessing.

blocks.text: Compare the complete workload

items: Begin without a prefix index; answer initial intervals by direct scan and record their visited lengths for the current source version.
After each query, evaluate a defined threshold using cumulative demand, the O(n) build cost, memory, version stability, and expected later compatible work.
If that policy triggers, construct exactly one prefix representation and bind it to the still-current version.
Route later compatible queries through prefix subtraction until a version change invalidates the representation.

blocks.text: Building before measuring demand defeats the purpose of a lazy policy. Rechecking the threshold without recording that construction finished can duplicate O(n) work, while reusing after a version change converts an optimization into a correctness bug. Observed past work is evidence for the policy, not a guarantee of future queries.

blocks.text: Do not choose a prefix array merely because there are several intervals. Count build time, the cost of all queries, the length of direct scans, memory, and whether the source changes. Prefix state is valuable when compatible static queries reuse it; a one-pass local workload usually gains more from direct or rolling state.

items.prompt: One range query spans m elements of an n-value array and no preprocessing exists. Select direct-scan time and auxiliary space.
constraints: The query answer is one scalar sum.

feedback.reason: The direct cost follows the queried interval length, not necessarily the full array size.

blocks.text: Compare the complete workload

Initialize one scalar sum and visit the m positions in the requested interval exactly once. Each visit performs constant-time read-and-add work, so m visits give O(m) time. The loop indices and running sum occupy a fixed number of machine words independent of m and n, so auxiliary space is O(1); the scalar answer does not require storing the interval. O(1) time would require an already available index, which the prompt excludes, while O(m) space would confuse inspected input values with newly allocated working memory. This O(m)-time baseline is what preprocessing must improve enough to repay its own build.

blocks.title: Preprocessing must earn its cost
blocks.text: Do not choose a prefix array merely because there are several intervals. Count build time, the cost of all queries, the length of direct scans, memory, and whether the source changes. Prefix state is valuable when compatible static queries reuse it; a one-pass local workload usually gains more from direct or rolling state.

items.prompt: q range queries have lengths m1 through mq and are answered by direct scans. Select total time and auxiliary space.
constraints: No query state is retained after its answer.

feedback.reason: Direct workload cost is the cumulative number of visited elements.

blocks.text: Compare the complete workload

Query i visits mi values and performs Θ(mi) additions. Because no state is retained to share work between queries, summing those costs gives Θ(m1 + ... + mq), reported as O(m1 + ... + mq). The same running-sum variable and loop indices are reused for every query, so peak auxiliary space remains O(1), not O(q) and not the total number of visits. The coarser O(qn) bound applies only as a worst-case upper bound because every mi is at most n; it is tight when all q intervals have length Θ(n), but it hides workloads made of short ranges.

blocks.title: Preprocessing must earn its cost
blocks.text: Do not choose a prefix array merely because there are several intervals. Count build time, the cost of all queries, the length of direct scans, memory, and whether the source changes. Prefix state is valuable when compatible static queries reuse it; a one-pass local workload usually gains more from direct or rolling state.

items.prompt: Build a prefix array for n static values and answer q scalar range-sum queries. Select total time and auxiliary space.
constraints: Each query uses two prefix reads and one subtraction.

feedback.reason: The build is linear and each compatible query is constant time.

blocks.text: Compare the complete workload

Construct P with n + 1 entries. Writing P[i + 1] = P[i] + a[i] for all n source values costs O(n) time and O(n) auxiliary space. Each of the q queries performs two prefix reads and one subtraction, so its cost is O(1) and all query work is O(q). Adding sequential phases yields O(n + q) total time, not O(q) because construction cannot be omitted and not O(qn) because intervals are no longer scanned. The prefix representation remains live throughout the workload, so peak auxiliary space is O(n); returning q scalar answers does not make the index O(qn).

blocks.title: Preprocessing must earn its cost
blocks.text: Do not choose a prefix array merely because there are several intervals. Count build time, the cost of all queries, the length of direct scans, memory, and whether the source changes. Prefix state is valuable when compatible static queries reuse it; a one-pass local workload usually gains more from direct or rolling state.

items.prompt: Compute every length-k block sum in one sequential pass with a rolling sum. Select total time and auxiliary space.
constraints: The first block is summed once.
Each later block uses one subtraction and one addition.
The input is an indexable array, so an outgoing value can be read by index.

feedback.reason: Sequential repeated intervals can be cheaper in memory than a reusable random-query index.

blocks.text: Compare the complete workload

The first length-k block takes O(k) additions. There are n - k later starting positions, and each shift performs one indexed subtraction, one indexed addition, and one output or comparison, all O(1). Total time is therefore O(k + (n - k)) = O(n). The current sum and indices are a constant number of variables, so auxiliary space is O(1); the source array supplies the outgoing value and reported outputs are not working state. In a non-rewindable stream, the same recurrence would require retaining up to k values to know what leaves, so the O(1)-space result depends on the prompt's indexable-array boundary.

blocks.title: Preprocessing must earn its cost
blocks.text: Do not choose a prefix array merely because there are several intervals. Count build time, the cost of all queries, the length of direct scans, memory, and whether the source changes. Prefix state is valuable when compatible static queries reuse it; a one-pass local workload usually gains more from direct or rolling state.

items.prompt: Each of q queries scans the entire n-value array. Compare direct scans with one prefix build and q scalar range queries. Select both total times.

feedback.reason: Full-range rescanning repeats n work q times.

blocks.text: Compare the complete workload

The stated direct implementation performs n constant-time visits for each of q queries, so its total is q·O(n) = O(qn). The prefix implementation visits n values once to build cumulative state and then spends O(1) on each of q subtractions, giving O(n) + q·O(1) = O(n + q). This comparison analyzes the two specified workloads; it is not advice to rescan an identical full-range answer that could simply be cached. The asymptotic improvement comes from replacing repeated interval visits with one reusable static representation, and it is legal only while the source version remains unchanged.

items.prompt: The system processes u complete source-array versions of length n. It builds one prefix array for each version and answers q scalar range queries in total. Select total time and peak prefix space.
constraints: Only one version's prefix array is live at a time.

feedback.reason: Version churn multiplies preprocessing cost by u.

blocks.text: Compare the complete workload

Every one of the u versions requires a full pass over n values, so rebuild work is u·O(n) = O(un). Across all versions, q constant-time prefix differences add O(q), producing O(un + q) total time. Only one length-(n + 1) prefix array is live at a time because the constraints release the previous version before retaining the next, so peak prefix space is O(n), not O(un). Confusing total allocations over the lifecycle with simultaneously live memory yields the larger wrong bound; omitting version churn yields O(n + q) and undercounts u - 1 complete builds.

items.prompt: A direct approach answers q intervals whose total scanned length is L. A prefix approach builds n values and answers q queries. Select the two workload times.
constraints: Each direct visit and each prefix/query arithmetic operation costs O(1).

feedback.reason: The correct break-even comparison is L versus n + q.

blocks.text: Compare the complete workload

By definition, the direct path performs exactly L constant-time element visits across all q intervals, so its total is O(L) with no separate qn assumption. The prefix path visits n source values once and performs constant-time arithmetic for each of q queries, so its total is O(n + q). The comparison is therefore L versus n + q, together with O(1) versus O(n) auxiliary state. Prefix work is asymptotically smaller when L grows beyond the build-plus-query term and the data stays valid; direct scans remain attractive when L is small, memory is constrained, or reuse may never occur.

contrastSets.transferBoundary: For one sequential objective, avoid preprocessing that is not reused; for many static interval queries, compare full prefix build-plus-query cost, while updates may invalidate the static prefix representation.
